neighbors.heading: a mustard seed
neighbors.text: Today Epictetus said: never say "I lost it," say "I gave it back." Buddhists tell of Kisa Gotami, who carried her dead little son from house to house, looking for medicine. The Buddha asked her for one mustard seed from a home where no one had ever died. She found none, and came to see that everything that comes into being also passes.
neighbors.difference: Epictetus pictures a giver who lends and takes back. The Buddha names no lender: all that arises passes away, and the way through grief is to stop clinging, even to a self that owns things.
neighbors.shared: you can hold what you love with open hands.
neighbors.sources: Dhammapada Commentary, the story of Kisa Gotami (verse 114) (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the lord gave
neighbors.text: Today Epictetus said: never say "I lost it," say "I gave it back." Catholics know an older voice. When Job lost his children and everything he had, he said: "The Lord gave, and the Lord hath taken away: as it hath pleased the Lord so is it done: blessed be the name of the Lord."
neighbors.difference: Epictetus asks for calm. Job first tore his garment and fell to the ground, and later cried out and argued with God. Catholics read Job as a man of faith who could grieve aloud before God.
neighbors.shared: the people we love are a gift, not a possession.

neighbors.heading: enjoy by letting go
neighbors.text: Today Epictetus said to live as at a banquet: take a modest share, and don't reach after the dish that passes. The Isha Upanishad opens in a similar key. All of this, it says, is covered by the Lord; enjoy it by letting go, and don't covet anyone's wealth.
neighbors.difference: Epictetus keeps desire small because the dish isn't up to you. The Upanishad sees the whole world filled with the Lord, so what you enjoy is received, not grabbed.
neighbors.shared: a modest share, received gladly, is a full meal.

neighbors.heading: rejoicing in your portion
neighbors.text: Today Epictetus said to live as at a banquet: take a modest share, and don't reach after the dish that passes. The rabbis asked about the same table. Ben Zoma said: who is rich? The one who rejoices in his portion. And the Torah says: "thou shalt eat and be satisfied, and bless the LORD thy God."
neighbors.difference: Epictetus asks for restraint, so desire can't rule you. Jewish tradition adds thanks: a blessing before eating and after, because the food comes from God, and a portion received with joy honors him.
neighbors.shared: a modest plate, met with joy, is a full one.

neighbors.heading: the other cheek
neighbors.text: Today Epictetus said an insult only harms you if you judge that it has. Jesus taught: "whosoever shall smite thee on thy right cheek, turn to him the other also." And he went further: "Love your enemies, bless them that curse you."
neighbors.difference: Epictetus guards your judgment, so the blow can't reach the inside. Jesus doesn't say the blow is nothing; he asks you to answer it with love, even to pray for the one who struck, as children of a Father kind to all.
neighbors.shared: an insult doesn't get to decide who you become.

neighbors.heading: answer: peace
neighbors.text: Today Epictetus said an insult only harms you if you judge that it has. The Qur'an describes the servants of the Merciful: they walk the earth modestly, "and when the foolish ones address them answer: Peace." It also says: "Repel the evil deed with one which is better," and an enemy may become a warm friend.
neighbors.difference: Epictetus treats the insult as finished inside your own judgment. The Qur'an allows a fair answer to a wrong, yet calls pardoning and making peace better, and says its reward is with God.
neighbors.shared: you can answer a sharp word with peace.

neighbors.heading: reckon the charges
neighbors.text: Today Epictetus said to look at what comes before and after anything you start, like an athlete before the games. Jesus told the crowds following him: "which of you having a mind to build a tower, doth not first sit down, and reckon the charges that are necessary, whether he have wherewithal to finish it."
neighbors.difference: Epictetus asks whether your own strength is enough. In Luke, the cost is following Jesus with your whole life, and Catholics trust that God's grace helps them pay what they couldn't alone.
neighbors.shared: a promise kept starts with an honest look at its cost.

neighbors.heading: head on your palm
neighbors.text: Today Epictetus said to count the cost before you begin, like an athlete before the games. Guru Nanak set the price of his path just as plainly: if you want to play the game of love, come to my lane with your head on your palm.
neighbors.difference: Epictetus counts the cost so you won't quit in shame halfway. For Guru Nanak, the price is the ego itself, laid down in love for God, and it's God's grace that makes it possible.
neighbors.shared: the deepest things ask for your whole heart.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1412, Guru Nanak (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: not a talebearer
neighbors.text: Today Epictetus said to speak rarely, only what's needed, and not about people. The Torah says: "Thou shalt not go up and down as a talebearer among thy people." And in the Mishnah, Shimon, son of Rabban Gamliel, says he grew up among the sages and found nothing better for the body than silence.
neighbors.difference: Epictetus keeps quiet to guard his own character. Jewish law also counts the harm to the one spoken about, and treats hurtful talk, even when true, as a wrong against a neighbor and before God.
neighbors.shared: a quiet tongue is a kindness to people not in the room.

neighbors.heading: the right time, the true word
neighbors.text: Today Epictetus said to speak rarely, only what's needed, and not about people. The Buddha taught right speech. A word is well spoken, he said, when it's spoken at the right time, it's true, it's gentle, it's helpful, and it comes from a mind of goodwill.
neighbors.difference: Epictetus makes silence the general rule. The Buddha's test isn't how little you say but what kind of word it is, and right speech is one step on the path to freedom from suffering.
neighbors.shared: before you speak, ask if it's true and if it's kind.

neighbors.heading: eat, and be not prodigal
neighbors.text: Today Epictetus said the body is the measure of what you need, as the foot is of the shoe. The Qur'an says: "eat and drink, but be not prodigal. Lo! He loveth not the prodigals." And a hadith gives a picture: a third of the stomach for food, a third for drink, a third for breath.
neighbors.difference: Epictetus lets the body set the limit. The Qur'an treats food as God's good provision, to enjoy with thanks; keeping to measure honors the Giver.
neighbors.shared: enough is a gift you can say thank you for.

neighbors.heading: not too much, not too little
neighbors.text: Today Epictetus said the body is the measure of what you need, as the foot is of the shoe. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna says yoga isn't for someone who eats too much or too little, or sleeps too much or too little. For one who is measured in food, rest and work, he says, yoga ends sorrow.
neighbors.difference: Epictetus measures need so the will stays free. Krishna's measure serves yoga: a steady body and mind, so a person can turn inward and toward God.
neighbors.shared: the body knows when it's enough; listen kindly.

neighbors.heading: truthful living
neighbors.text: Today Epictetus said sheep don't show the shepherd how much they ate; they show wool. Don't talk about your principles; live them. Guru Nanak said it in one line: truth is higher than everything, but higher still is truthful living.
neighbors.difference: Epictetus wants deeds over talk so you won't be a showman. For Guru Nanak, truthful living grows from remembering God's Name, and it's lived in an ordinary life of honest work and sharing.
neighbors.shared: people learn more from how you live than from what you say.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 62, Guru Nanak (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: by their fruits
neighbors.text: Today Epictetus said sheep don't show the shepherd how much they ate; they show wool. Don't talk about your principles; live them. Jesus used a tree for the same idea: "Ye shall know them by their fruits." And the letter of James says: "shew me thy faith without thy works, and I will shew thee my faith by my works."
neighbors.difference: For Epictetus, deeds show a mind trained by reason. For Christians, good fruit grows from faith in Christ and the Spirit at work; works show faith, they don't earn God's love.
neighbors.shared: let your life say what words can't.

neighbors.heading: the simile of the saw
neighbors.text: Today Epictetus said a tyrant can chain his leg, but not even Zeus can conquer his will. The Buddha gave a harder picture. Even if bandits were cutting you limb from limb with a saw, he said, anyone whose mind turned to hatred wouldn't be following his teaching. Keep the mind unshaken, and full of goodwill, even toward them.
neighbors.difference: Epictetus holds the will as his own, out of anyone's reach. The Buddha asks for more than firmness: goodwill toward the one doing harm, and he doesn't treat the mind as a self you own.
neighbors.shared: what's deepest in you can't be chained.

neighbors.heading: they cannot kill the soul
neighbors.text: Today Epictetus said a tyrant can chain his leg, but not even Zeus can conquer his will. Jesus told his friends: "fear ye not them that kill the body, and are not able to kill the soul." The Church remembers martyrs who stood calm before rulers, trusting that what mattered most was safe.
neighbors.difference: For Epictetus, the will is free by its own nature. Catholics say the soul is safe because God holds it, the God who notices every sparrow; that freedom is a gift kept in his hands.
neighbors.shared: the deepest part of you can't be locked away.

neighbors.heading: the same in all
neighbors.text: Today Epictetus told a master: your slave is your brother, born of the same Zeus. The Bhagavad Gita says the wise see the same in a learned Brahmin, a cow, an elephant, a dog, and an outcaste. Krishna says the yogi sees the Self in every being, and every being in the Self.
neighbors.difference: Epictetus finds kinship in the reason every person shares. The Gita sees one Self in all beings, animals too, and teaches that seeing it changes how you treat everyone.
neighbors.shared: no one is beneath you; everyone is kin.

neighbors.heading: one father
neighbors.text: Today Epictetus told a master: your slave is your brother, born of the same Zeus. A Hebrew prophet asked the same question: "Have we not all one father? Hath not one God created us? Why do we deal treacherously every man against his brother?"
neighbors.difference: Epictetus's Zeus is the reason running through nature. Malachi's one father is the one God who created each person, and the Torah gave servants the Sabbath's rest too.
neighbors.shared: the one who serves you is your brother or sister.

neighbors.heading: the temple within
neighbors.text: Today Epictetus said that when you shut the door and darken the room, you're not alone: God is within. Paul wrote to the Christians at Corinth: "Know ye not that ye are the temple of God, and that the Spirit of God dwelleth in you?" And Jesus promised: "lo, I am with you alway."
neighbors.difference: For Epictetus, God is the reason running through all things, present in each of us. Christians speak of the Holy Spirit dwelling in believers: a personal God who knows and loves them by name.
neighbors.shared: even in a dark, quiet room, you're not alone.

neighbors.heading: nearer than the jugular
neighbors.text: Today Epictetus said that when you shut the door and darken the room, you're not alone. The Qur'an says of every person: "We know what his soul whispereth to him, and We are nearer to him than his jugular vein." And: "He is with you wheresoever ye may be."
neighbors.difference: Epictetus says God is within you, a share of the divine. In Islam, God is closer than your own vein in knowing and care, yet never part of you; the Creator stays One, beyond all he made.
neighbors.shared: no door shuts you away from being known.

neighbors.heading: virtue is a habit
neighbors.text: Today Epictetus said every habit grows by the actions that match it: walk to become a walker. The Catholic Church teaches the same about goodness. Its Catechism calls virtue a habitual and firm disposition to do good, and says human virtues are gained by education, deliberate acts and perseverance, again and again.
neighbors.difference: Epictetus builds character by practice alone. Catholics say that too for human virtues, but faith, hope and love are gifts poured in by God's grace, which also helps the practice along.
neighbors.shared: every small good act makes the next one easier.

neighbors.heading: you sow, you eat
neighbors.text: Today Epictetus said every habit grows by the actions that match it: walk to become a walker. In the Japji, Guru Nanak says good and bad aren't just words we say; our deeds are written down, and what we sow, we ourselves eat. When the mind is soiled, he says, love of God's Name washes it clean.
neighbors.difference: Epictetus says practice alone makes you who you are. Guru Nanak gives deeds real weight, but says the door of liberation opens by God's grace, not by effort alone.
neighbors.shared: what you practice today, you become.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 2 and Ang 4, Japji 4 and 20, Guru Nanak (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: love that doesn't depend
neighbors.text: Today Epictetus said friendship fails when two people want the same piece of meat. The Mishnah says something close: love that depends on a thing ends when the thing is gone; love that depends on nothing never ends. Its example of the lasting kind is David and Jonathan, whose souls, the Bible says, were knit together.
neighbors.difference: Epictetus says only those who place the good in their own will can be friends. David and Jonathan sealed their friendship as a covenant before God, a bond held by faithfulness, not only by right judgment.
neighbors.shared: a real friend wants you, not what you can give.

neighbors.heading: the good friend
neighbors.text: Today Epictetus said friendship fails when two people want the same piece of meat. The Buddha told a young man named Sigala how to tell friends apart. The false friend only takes, or only flatters. The true one helps, stays the same in good times and bad, tells you what's good for you, and cares.
neighbors.difference: Epictetus sees friendship as the fruit of a mind already set right. The Buddha called good friendship the whole of the holy life: not only the reward of the path, but part of how you walk it.
neighbors.shared: a real friend wants you, not what you can give.
neighbors.sources: Digha Nikaya 31, Sigalovada Sutta; Samyutta Nikaya 45.2 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: every post a trust
neighbors.text: Today Epictetus said each life is like military service: one stands guard, one scouts, and you stay at the post you've been given. The Qur'an says God has placed people as viceroys of the earth, "and hath exalted some of you in rank above others, that He may try you by (the test of) that which He hath given you."
neighbors.difference: Epictetus asks you to trust the general and serve well. In the Qur'an, every post is a trust and a test from God, and each person answers to him for how they used what they were given.
neighbors.shared: there's no small post when it's held faithfully.

neighbors.heading: your own duty
neighbors.text: Today Epictetus said to stay at the post you've been given, like a soldier. The Bhagavad Gita begins with a real soldier, Arjuna, wanting to leave his post. Krishna tells him: better your own duty, even done imperfectly, than another's done well.
neighbors.difference: Epictetus serves at his post because the general knows best. Krishna asks Arjuna to act without clinging to the results, offering the work itself to God, so the post becomes a path to freedom.
neighbors.shared: there's no small post when it's held faithfully.

neighbors.heading: contentment holds the earth
neighbors.text: Today Seneca said the poor person isn't the one with too little, but the one who craves more. Guru Nanak's Japji has an old picture: the bull said to hold up the earth is dharma, born of compassion, and contentment holds it patiently in place.
neighbors.difference: Seneca reasons his way to wanting less. For Sikhs, contentment grows from living in God's will and remembering the Name, by grace, and it goes hand in hand with honest work and sharing.
neighbors.shared: enough, held gladly, makes anyone rich.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 3, Japji 16, Guru Nanak (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: learned to be content
neighbors.text: Today Seneca said the poor person isn't the one with too little, but the one who craves more. Paul wrote, while in chains: "I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content." And to Timothy: "godliness with contentment is great gain."
neighbors.difference: Seneca finds contentment in a mind that needs nothing more. Paul names where his strength comes from: "I can do all things through Christ which strengtheneth me."
neighbors.shared: enough, held gladly, makes anyone rich.

neighbors.heading: from craving, fear
neighbors.text: Today Seneca said hope and fear are chained together, like a prisoner and his guard. The Dhammapada traces both to one root: "From greed comes grief, from greed comes fear; he who is free from greed knows neither grief nor fear."
neighbors.difference: Seneca's cure is to live in the present and stop leaning on tomorrow. The Buddha's is the ending of craving itself, which the path loosens step by step, until even clinging to a self that hopes falls away.
neighbors.shared: this moment is a safe place to stand.

neighbors.heading: sufficient for the day
neighbors.text: Today Seneca said hope and fear are chained together: both run ahead to tomorrow. Jesus told the crowds: "Be not therefore solicitous for to morrow; for the morrow will be solicitous for itself. Sufficient for the day is the evil thereof."
neighbors.difference: Seneca says stop hoping and you'll stop fearing. Catholics keep hope as a virtue, one of three God gives, but move it off tomorrow's outcomes and onto God himself.
neighbors.shared: today has enough in it; let tomorrow wait.
neighbors.sources: Matthew 6:34 (Douay-Rheims); Catechism of the Catholic Church 1817 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the witness within
neighbors.text: Today Seneca passed on a rule: live among people as if God saw you. The Shvetashvatara Upanishad speaks of one God hidden in all beings, filling everything, the inner Self of all, who watches over every deed: the witness.
neighbors.difference: Seneca's rule is a practice, living as if watched. For the Upanishad, the witness isn't an eye outside you; it's the one God, the inner Self of every being.
neighbors.shared: live the same whether or not anyone's looking.

neighbors.heading: an eye that sees
neighbors.text: Today Seneca passed on a rule: live among people as if God saw you. The Mishnah says it without the "as if": know what is above you, an eye that sees, an ear that hears, and all your deeds written in a book. Keep that in mind, it says, and you won't fall into wrongdoing.
neighbors.difference: For Seneca, the watcher is a picture that helps. For the Mishnah, God truly sees and remembers, and Jewish tradition holds that the same God welcomes return and forgives.
neighbors.shared: be the same person in the dark as in the light.

neighbors.heading: i die daily
neighbors.text: Today Seneca said we die every day: each day, a little of life is taken away. Paul wrote almost the same words to the Christians at Corinth: "I die daily." He meant he faced danger every day for the gospel, and he wrote it in a chapter about rising again.
neighbors.difference: Seneca counts the days so we'll use them well and fear the end less. Paul faces each day's dying in the hope of resurrection: "O death, where is thy sting?"
neighbors.shared: each day is a gift; spend it on what matters.

neighbors.heading: a stranger, a traveler
neighbors.text: Today Seneca said we die every day, so treat each one as precious. The Prophet Muhammad told Ibn Umar: be in this world as if you were a stranger, or a traveler passing through. Ibn Umar added: in the evening, don't wait for the morning; take from your health for your sickness, and from your life for your death.
neighbors.difference: Seneca leaves open what comes after. For Muslims, the traveler is going home to God, and the days given here are a trust to fill with good, to be met again in the Hereafter.
neighbors.shared: travel light, and use today well.

neighbors.heading: more inward than my inmost
neighbors.text: Today Seneca wrote: "God is near you, he is with you, he is within you." Saint Augustine, writing his Confessions as a prayer, found the same nearness. He said to God: "Thou wert more inward to me than my most inward part; and higher than my highest."
neighbors.difference: Seneca's god within sounds like a share of divine reason in us. For Augustine, God is closer than our inmost self yet higher than our highest: the Creator, never a part of us.
neighbors.shared: you're closer to the holy than you know.

neighbors.heading: you are light
neighbors.text: Today Seneca wrote that God is near you, with you, within you. Guru Amar Das speaks to his own mind: O my mind, you are the very form of divine light; know your source. And Guru Nanak sings that one light is in everyone, and that light is God's.
neighbors.difference: Seneca reaches the god within by reason and a good character. In Sikh teaching, the light is in all, and it's recognized through the Guru's word and remembering God's Name, by grace.
neighbors.shared: there's a light in you, and in everyone you meet.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 441, Guru Amar Das; Ang 13, Guru Nanak (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: remember egypt
neighbors.text: Today Seneca said: treat those beneath you as you'd want to be treated by those above. The Torah grounds the same care in memory: "And thou shalt remember that thou wast a bondman in the land of Egypt." And Hillel taught: what is hateful to you, don't do to your neighbor; that is the whole Torah.
neighbors.difference: Seneca reminds you that fortune could flip. The Torah gives a story and a command: you were slaves, God freed you, so treat the stranger and the servant as one who remembers.
neighbors.shared: remember when you were small, and be kind to the small.

neighbors.heading: they are like you
neighbors.text: Today Seneca said: treat those beneath you as you'd want to be treated by those above. The Dhammapada puts it in the plainest terms: "All men tremble at punishment, all men fear death; remember that you are like unto them, and do not kill, nor cause slaughter."
neighbors.difference: Seneca argues from fortune, which could put you below tomorrow. The Buddha argues from the fear of pain we all share, and widens the circle past people, to every living being.
neighbors.shared: everyone fears pain just as you do; be gentle.

neighbors.heading: the bee's path
neighbors.text: Today Seneca said to read like the bees: gather from many flowers, then make honey that is your own. The Qur'an has a chapter named The Bee. God inspires the bee to "eat of all fruits, and follow the ways of thy Lord," and from it comes "a drink divers of hues, wherein is healing for mankind."
neighbors.difference: Seneca's bee is a picture of reading and blending. In the Qur'an the bee is a sign: it follows paths its Lord made smooth, and the honey calls people to reflect on him.
neighbors.shared: gather the good wherever it grows.

neighbors.heading: the bee and the scriptures
neighbors.text: Today Seneca said to read like the bees: gather from many flowers, then make honey that is your own. The Bhagavata Purana tells of a wandering sage who learned from the world around him, the bee among his teachers. As the bee takes nectar from many flowers, he says, the wise take the essence from every teaching, great and small.
neighbors.difference: Seneca's honey is your own good judgment. For the Bhagavata, the essence gathered is knowledge of the Self and love of God, and the sage's freedom comes from that, not from reading alone.
neighbors.shared: gather the good wherever it grows.

neighbors.heading: children of the one
neighbors.text: Today Seneca wrote: we are the limbs of one great body; nature made us kin. Guru Arjan sang: the One is our father, and we are all the One's children. Sikhs live it at the langar, the free kitchen, where everyone sits together on the floor and eats the same meal.
neighbors.difference: Seneca's kinship comes from nature, which made us of the same stuff. For Sikhs, it comes from one Creator, and it's lived out in seva, service, to anyone who walks in.
neighbors.shared: everyone at the table is family.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 611, Guru Arjan (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: many members, one body
neighbors.text: Today Seneca wrote: we are the limbs of one great body. Paul used the same picture for the church: "For as the body is one, and hath many members... so also is Christ." And: "whether one member suffer, all the members suffer with it; or one member be honoured, all the members rejoice with it."
neighbors.difference: Seneca's body is all of humankind, joined by nature. Paul's body is Christ's, joined by the Spirit, though Christians also hold that every person is made in God's image.
neighbors.shared: when one of us hurts, we all do.

neighbors.heading: the best riches
neighbors.text: Today Seneca said the rich person is the one who has little and wants nothing more. The Dhammapada says: "Health is the greatest of gifts, contentedness the best riches; trust is the best of relationships, Nirvana the highest happiness."
neighbors.difference: Seneca's riches are a mind that needs nothing more. The Dhammapada sets contentment beside a further goal, Nirvana, the end of craving and suffering, which the path walks toward.
neighbors.shared: the best things you own can't be carried in a parade.

neighbors.heading: treasure in heaven
neighbors.text: Today Seneca said the rich person is the one who has little and wants nothing more. Jesus said: "Lay not up to yourselves treasures on earth: where the rust, and moth consume, and where thieves break through and steal." Store treasure in heaven instead, he said, "For where thy treasure is, there is thy heart also."
neighbors.difference: Seneca keeps his riches inside, in a mind content with little. Jesus points the heart toward God, and Catholics see giving to the poor as one way of storing up that treasure.
neighbors.shared: what your heart treasures is what you truly have.

neighbors.heading: bring the mind back
neighbors.text: Today Seneca said restless people keep changing places, fleeing themselves. In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna gives Arjuna a gentle practice: wherever the restless, unsteady mind wanders off, draw it back, and let it rest in the Self.
neighbors.difference: Seneca's cure is to make peace with your own company. Krishna's is to come home to the Self, which the Gita teaches is deeper than the restless mind, and to God.
neighbors.shared: you can stop running and come home to yourself.

neighbors.heading: whither shall i flee
neighbors.text: Today Seneca said restless people keep changing places, fleeing themselves. Jonah tried running too; he "rose up to flee unto Tarshish from the presence of the LORD." And a psalm asks: "Whither shall I go from Thy spirit? Or whither shall I flee from Thy presence?"
neighbors.difference: Seneca says you can't outrun yourself. The psalmist finds you can't outrun God, and takes comfort in it: even at the far end of the sea, "even there would Thy hand lead me."
neighbors.shared: you can stop running; what you need is already here.

neighbors.heading: slow to wrath
neighbors.text: Today Seneca said the greatest remedy for anger is delay. The letter of James says: "let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath: For the wrath of man worketh not the righteousness of God." And Paul: "let not the sun go down upon your wrath."
neighbors.difference: Seneca wants anger gone entirely. Paul writes "Be ye angry, and sin not," so anger isn't always wrong; the danger is holding on to it, and his cure is forgiving as God forgave you.
neighbors.shared: a pause between the spark and the words is a gift.

neighbors.heading: sit down, then lie down
neighbors.text: Today Seneca said the greatest remedy for anger is delay. The Qur'an praises "those who control their wrath and are forgiving toward mankind." And the Prophet Muhammad gave a practical tip: if you're angry while standing, sit down; if the anger hasn't left, lie down.
neighbors.difference: Seneca's delay lets reason judge calmly. The Qur'an pairs holding back anger with forgiving, and says God loves those who do good.
neighbors.shared: a pause between the spark and the words is a gift.

neighbors.heading: the mote and the beam
neighbors.text: Today Seneca said that if we look honestly at our own faults, we'll be gentler with others'. Jesus asked: "why seest thou the mote that is in thy brother's eye; and seest not the beam that is in thy own eye?" And: "Judge not, and you shall not be judged."
neighbors.difference: Seneca's reason is fairness: no one could be acquitted of everything. Jesus adds mercy: forgive, and you will be forgiven, because God's mercy toward us is the measure for ours.
neighbors.shared: go easy on others; you've needed grace too.

neighbors.heading: i am the worst of all
neighbors.text: Today Seneca said that if we look honestly at our own faults, we'll be gentler with others'. Kabir, whose verses are in the Sikh scripture, says: of all people, I am the bad one; everyone but me is good. Whoever understands it this way, he says, is my friend.
neighbors.difference: Seneca's honesty about faults is a matter of fair judgment. In Sikh teaching, humility like Kabir's is part of devotion: the ego steps aside so God's love can fill the heart.
neighbors.shared: go easy on others; you've needed grace too.

neighbors.heading: giving as justice
neighbors.text: Today Seneca said to give freely, promptly, and without reminding. Maimonides set out the ways of giving tzedakah, from lower to higher. Higher is giving gladly, giving before you're asked, giving so neither side knows the other; highest is helping someone stand on their own, with a gift, a loan, or work.
neighbors.difference: For Seneca, a benefit is a free favor that binds friends. Tzedakah shares its root with the Hebrew word for justice: giving to the poor is a duty owed, not only a kindness.
neighbors.shared: give with an open hand and a quiet mouth.
neighbors.sources: Maimonides, Mishneh Torah, Gifts to the Poor 10:7-14 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the good person's gift
neighbors.text: Today Seneca said to give freely, promptly, and without reminding. The Buddha described a good person's gift: given with trust, given with care, given at the right time, given with a heart that doesn't cling, and given without hurting yourself or anyone else.
neighbors.difference: Seneca's benefit ties giver and receiver together in gratitude. In the Buddha's teaching, giving, dana, is practice in letting go, loosening craving in the one who gives.
neighbors.shared: give with an open hand and a quiet mouth.
